title: Minimum Operations to Reduce X to Zero
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every end-removal combination versus a sliding window on the complementary middle target.

content.title: Minimum Operations to Reduce X to Zero

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and an integer x, find the minimum number of elements that must be removed from either the very left end or the very right end of the array (some combination of both) so that the sum of all removed elements equals exactly x. Return -1 if this is not possible.

blocks.caption: Reframe as finding the longest kept middle subarray summing to the total minus x

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and an integer x, find the minimum number of elements that must be removed from either the very left end or the very right end of the array (some combination of both) so that the sum of all removed elements equals exactly x. Return -1 if this is not possible.

blocks.title: Analogy: Trimming a Ribbon From Both Ends to Reach an Exact Total Length
blocks.text: Like snipping pieces off both ends of a marked ribbon, alternating or favoring either end as needed, until the total length snipped off matches an exact target, using as few snips as possible.

blocks.caption: Remove elements from either end so their sum equals x, using as few removals as possible

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Removing the last two elements: 2 plus 3 equals 5","exactly the target, using 2 removals","Taking exactly the rightmost two elements sums precisely to the target x, and no smaller combination of end-removals achieves this"],["Answer","2","2 total removals is the minimum needed to reach a removed-sum of exactly 5"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["No combination of elements from either end ever sums to exactly 4","impossible","Every individual element already exceeds 4, so even a single removal from either end overshoots the target, and no combination can land exactly on it"],["Answer","-1","No valid combination of end-removals exists at all"]]}

blocks.text: Removing 3, 2, and 1, 1, 3 from both ends (three from the left, two from the right) sums to exactly 10, needing 5 total removals.

Before trying every combination of left-count and right-count removals, notice a removal from both ends of an array always leaves behind exactly one contiguous middle piece, and reasoning about that single leftover piece is far simpler than reasoning about two separate, simultaneously-shrinking ends.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If some elements are removed from the left and some from the right, whatever remains is always a single, unbroken, contiguous subarray sitting in the middle, no matter how the removal counts on each side are chosen.

Observation 2: The elements removed sum to x by definition, and the elements remaining sum to the total sum of nums minus x, since removed and remaining together make up the entire array's total exactly once.

Observation 3: Minimizing the number of elements removed is exactly the same goal as maximizing the number of elements kept, since removed count plus kept count always equals n, the fixed total length of the array.

Observation 4: So the entire problem reduces to finding the longest contiguous subarray whose sum equals the total sum minus x; since every element is positive, a sliding window works directly here, growing the sum can only ever increase it, letting the window shrink from the left whenever it overshoots, with no ambiguity about which direction to move.

Whenever a problem asks to remove elements from both ends of an array to hit some target, reframe it immediately as "find the longest, or shortest, contiguous middle subarray hitting the complementary target", since the leftover middle is always contiguous and often much easier to search directly.

This reframing is what turns an awkward two-ended combinatorial search into the extremely standard "longest subarray with a given sum, all positive elements" sliding window problem, which has a clean, well-known solution.

Try every possible number of elements removed from the left, combined with every possible number removed from the right, computing the sum removed for each combination and checking whether it equals x.

items: For every possible count of elements removed from the left, and every possible count removed from the right, without overlapping, compute their combined sum.
If that sum equals x, track the total number of elements removed, keeping the smallest.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The right removal count's upper bound depends on how many were already removed from the left, ensuring the two removed regions never overlap, together removing at most all n elements.
removed_sum is recomputed directly from the array slices each time, rather than incrementally, since this version prioritizes clarity over efficiency.
best is only updated when removed_sum exactly equals x, and only if the new total is smaller than any found so far, directly implementing the "minimum operations" requirement.

blocks.text: Every possible combination of left and right removal counts is directly checked, so the minimum valid total is correctly found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed) in the most naive form (recomputing sums each time), or O(n squared) with prefix sums.
Space: O(1) extra beyond simple prefix sum arrays.

Limitation: removing from both ends to sum exactly x is equivalent to leaving a contiguous middle subarray whose sum equals the total sum minus x, and finding the longest such middle subarray directly, using a sliding window, is far more efficient than trying every combination of end counts.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force tries every independent combination of left-count and right-count, but that independence is itself the waste: once the total number removed is fixed, the specific split between left and right does not need to be searched at all, it only needs the sum of the two removed regions to hit x, and that sum's complement, the sum of whatever remains in the middle, is a single well-defined target. Since every element is positive, growing a candidate middle window can only increase its sum, and shrinking it can only decrease it, exactly the monotonic property a sliding window needs to know unambiguously which direction fixes an overshoot. Searching directly for the longest window hitting the complementary target replaces two independent nested loops over removal counts with one linear scan over possible middle-subarray boundaries.

Removing some elements from the left and some from the right is exactly equivalent to keeping a single contiguous subarray in the middle. Since removing fewer elements overall means keeping a longer middle subarray, minimizing removals is the same as maximizing the length of a middle subarray whose sum equals the total sum of nums minus x. Since all elements are positive, this maximum length subarray can be found using a standard sliding window: expand the window to grow the sum, shrink it from the left whenever the sum exceeds the target, and track the longest window whose sum exactly matches.
Find the longest subarray summing to the total sum minus x using a sliding window, then the answer is n minus that length.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Total sum of nums","1 + 1 + 4 + 2 + 3 = 11","The total sum is needed to compute the complementary target that the kept middle subarray must reach"],["Target middle sum: total minus x","11 minus 5 equals 6","Whatever remains after removing elements summing to x must, by definition, sum to the total minus x"],["Longest subarray summing to 6","[1, 1, 4] (length 3)","This is the longest contiguous run of elements, found via the sliding window, whose sum exactly equals the target of 6"],["Answer: n minus that length","5 minus 3 equals 2","Removing everything outside this longest kept subarray requires exactly n minus its length removals, matching the minimum found directly"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: find the longest middle subarray summing to total minus x, then subtract its length from n

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single sliding window pass.
Space: O(1) extra.

Because every element in nums is positive, extending the window's right boundary can only increase current_sum, and shrinking its left boundary can only decrease it, so the shrink loop always has an unambiguous, correct direction to move whenever the sum overshoots the target: pull the left boundary inward until it no longer does. Every time current_sum lands exactly on target, the window's length is a genuinely valid candidate for the longest kept middle subarray, and tracking the maximum such length across the entire single pass guarantees the true longest one is found, since the window only ever grows or shrinks monotonically, never skipping over a valid configuration.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Special case","Correct handling"],"rows":[["target is negative (x is larger than the total sum)","Immediately impossible, since no subarray sum can ever be negative; return -1 directly without running the window search"],["target is exactly 0","The entire array itself is the longest, and only, valid \"kept\" subarray, since removing nothing at all leaves a remaining sum of 0 only when x equals the total"]]}

items: target is computed once, up front, as total minus x, converting the original two-ended removal question into a single-target subarray-length question.

The negative-target and zero-target cases are both handled explicitly before the main sliding window loop begins, since a negative target has no valid window at all, and a zero target is trivially satisfied by the whole array.
The shrink loop always runs to completion before checking for a match, ensuring current_sum never remains above target when the length comparison happens.

The final answer converts the best kept-length back into a removal count via the array length minus best_length, translating the "longest kept subarray" result back into the original problem's "minimum removed elements" question.

blocks.text: The core insight is reframing "remove from both ends to hit a target sum" as "keep the longest middle subarray hitting a complementary target sum", which converts an awkward two ended removal problem directly into the much more standard sliding window maximum length subarray pattern.

items: Forgetting to handle the target being negative, when x is larger than the total sum, which makes the answer immediately -1 without any window search needed, since no subarray can ever sum to a negative target.

Not handling the target being exactly 0 as its own case, where removing nothing at all, keeping the whole array, is trivially the best, and only, middle subarray, a case the general sliding window logic still handles correctly but is worth reasoning through explicitly.

Forgetting to convert the final "longest kept length" back into the original problem's "removed element count" by subtracting from n, and instead returning the kept length directly as if it were the answer.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["x equal to the total sum of the array","Requires every single element to be removed, corresponding to a target middle sum of 0, so the answer becomes n minus 0, meaning n"],["x equal to 0","The minimum number of operations is trivially 0, needing no removals at all, corresponding to a target middle sum equal to the full total, so the entire array is the longest kept subarray"]]}

items: State the reframing explicitly before writing any code: "removing from both ends to sum to x" is equivalent to "keeping the longest middle subarray summing to total minus x", since this reframing is the entire problem solving insight.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Remove elements from both ends of an array to hit a target" points toward reframing to "find the longest, or shortest, contiguous middle subarray hitting the complementary target", since two-ended removal always leaves one contiguous piece behind.

items: How would this change if nums could contain negative numbers? The sliding window's monotonic growing or shrinking property would break, since adding a negative number can decrease the sum; a different technique, such as a prefix-sum hash map, would be needed instead.

How would you also return which elements to remove, not just the count? Track the actual left and right boundary indices of the best kept window found, then everything outside those boundaries, on both sides, is exactly what should be removed.

What if the goal were to maximize the number of elements removed instead of minimizing, while still summing to exactly x? This becomes "find the shortest middle subarray summing to the complementary target" instead of the longest, though the underlying sliding window mechanics stay largely the same.
Same "reframe two-ended removal as one contiguous middle piece" insight is broadly useful whenever a problem describes trimming from both ends of a sequence.

Same monotonic sliding window technique, all positive elements, unambiguous shrink direction, as Subarrays with K Different Integers' atMost(k) building block and classic "longest subarray with sum at most or equal to target" problems.

Same "total minus removed equals kept, so minimizing one maximizes the other" complementary-quantity reasoning used whenever a problem's natural framing, minimize X, is harder to search directly than its complement, maximize total minus X.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) to O(n cubed) time depending on implementation, O(1) extra space.
Optimized (sliding window on the complementary target): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Reframe two-ended removal as finding the longest contiguous middle subarray summing to the complementary target
Core Idea: Minimizing elements removed from both ends is equivalent to maximizing the length of the kept middle subarray, whose sum must equal the total sum minus x
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1) extra

Most Important Observation: Removing from both ends of an array always leaves exactly one contiguous piece behind, turning an awkward two-ended search into a standard single-subarray sliding window problem
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Minimize removed from both ends equals maximize the kept middle summing to total minus x
